fetched_contents.text: Outcomes with Hematopoietic Stem Cell Transplantation in Secondary Hemophagocytic Lymphohistiocytosis: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis Background: Secondary hemophagocytic lymphohistiocytosis (HLH) is a disorder characterized by the hyper-stimulation of the immune system. HLH has a poor prognosis with up to a 100% mortality without an adequate therapy. Contrary to primary HLH, an efficient management approach has yet to be established for secondary HLH in adults. We conducted a systematic review and meta-analysis to evaluate the efficacy and safety of hematopoietic stem cell transplantation (HSCT) in this context. Methods Following the preferred reporting items for systemic reviews and Mata-analysis (PRISMA) guidelines, a comprehensive literature search was performed on 4 databases (PubMed, Cochrane Register of Controlled Trials, Embase and Clinicaltrials.gov) using MeSH terms and keywords for “Lymphohistiocytosis, Hemophagocytic” AND “Hematopoietic stem cell transplantation” AND “Therapeutics” AND “Treatment Outcome” from the date of inception to June 2021. Our search produced 2346 results and duplicates were removed. After excluding irrelevant and review articles during primary and secondary screening, seven original studies reporting HSCT as the treatment for secondary HLH in pediatric and adult patient population were included. The methodological quality of the included studies was evaluated using NIH quality assessment tool. Inter-study variance was calculated using the Der Simonian-Laird Estimator. Proportions along with 95% confidence Interval (CI) were extracted to compute pooled analysis using the ‘meta’ package by Schwarzer et al. in the R programming language (version 4.16-2). Results: A total of 136 patients from 7 studies were included. The median age of the patients was 32 (0.5-77) years and 57.4% (62/108) were males as reported by 4 studies. (Table 1) Allogeneic HSCT was used as a treatment modality for 100% (n=136) of the patients. The median time from diagnosis to HSCT was 4.9 (0.1-24) months as reported by 3 studies and median follow-up time was 22 (3-192) months as reported by 4 studies. The pooled overall response rate (ORR) after HSCT was 80% (95% CI 0.66-0.91, I 2 =21%, n=59) with pooled complete response (CR) of 54.5% (95% CI 0.19-0.87, I 2 =86%, n=59) and pooled partial response (PR) of 22.4% (95% CI 0.04-47, I 2 =72%, n=59). At a median follow-up of 30 (3-120) months, the pooled overall survival (OS) was 78.8% (95% CI 0.67-0.89, I 2 =41%, n=136). The pooled relapse rate (RR) was 12.2% (95 CI 0.045-0.22, I 2 =0%, n=61). The pooled incidence of acute graft versus host disease (GVHD) grade I/II and grade III/IV was 37.5% (95% CI 0.24-0.51, I 2 =0%, n=48) and 19.8% (95% CI 0.09-0.32, I 2 =0%, n=50) respectively, while pooled incidence of chronic GVHD was 26% (95% CI 0.13-0.41, I 2 =25%, n=50). Conclusion: HSCT shows excellent response rates and survival in patients with secondary HLH with an acceptable safety profile and should be considered. However, it is imperative that large prospective studies should be done to consolidate these findings. Clinical and laboratory features that distinguish HLH from non-HLH post-HCT patients

The strongest evidence here is that HLH is a hyperinflammatory syndrome with a specific clinical and laboratory profile that distinguishes it from common febrile complications after allogeneic HCT. The literature repeatedly frames HLH as a “life-threatening hyperinflammatory syndrome” characterized by inappropriate survival of histiocytes and failure of normal cytolytic functions of NK cells and CTL, while the non-HLH febrile complications include GVHD, sepsis, and other cytokine storm-like states [N1-R1][N4-R1][N4-R2]. This distinction is important because the clinical presentation may overlap, but the underlying pathophysiology differs: HLH is a macrophage activation syndrome, whereas GVHD is an alloreactive immune response, and sepsis is infection-driven inflammation [N4-R1][N4-R2][N4-R5].

The most predictive clinical signs and symptoms of HLH after allogeneic HCT are fever, splenomegaly, and cytopenia. The N3 search evidence shows that the revised HLH-2004 criteria require fever, splenomegaly, and cytopenia involving at least two of three lineages [N3-R1]. The same evidence also notes that typical findings of HLH include fever, hepatosplenomegaly, cytopenia, hypertriglyceridemia, and elevated ferritin or interleukin-2 receptor [N3-R3][N3-R4]. The N1 evidence adds that HLH is a rare, life-threatening syndrome characterized by hyperactivation of cytotoxic T lymphocytes and inappropriate histiocyte survival, which supports the view that HLH is not merely a “fever-cytopenia” entity but a broader systemic activation syndrome [N1-R5]. By contrast, the N4 evidence emphasizes that graft-versus-host disease is one of the most important and potentially fatal complications of allo-HSCT, and that febrile complications after HCT can resemble hyperacute GVHD, marrow aplasia, and transfusion-associated GVHD [N4-R1][N4-R4]. This means that fever, cytopenia, and organ involvement are not pathognomonic for HLH, but they are highly suggestive when combined with other HLH-specific features.

Laboratory biomarkers are central to distinguishing HLH from other post-HCT complications. The N3 evidence explicitly states that ferritin levels >500 ng/mL are used as a criterion for HLH diagnosis, though it notes that adult HLH patients typically do not meet the same pediatric thresholds as strongly as pediatric studies [N3-R2]. This is clinically important because ferritin can be elevated in many febrile post-HCT states, including GVHD, sepsis, and cytokine storm, making it a non-specific marker. The N3 evidence also points to elevated interleukin-2 receptor and hypertriglyceridemia as typical HLH findings [N3-R4]. The N1 evidence adds that HLH is characterized by inappropriate survival of histiocytes and failure of normal cytolytic functions, which supports the idea that biomarkers reflecting immune activation and tissue infiltration are more specific than fever or cytopenia alone [N1-R1]. In practice, therefore, HLH diagnosis depends on a combination of fever, cytopenia, organ enlargement, and laboratory markers rather than any single abnormality [N3-R1][N3-R2][N3-R3][N3-R4].

Imaging findings are also relevant. The N3 evidence on post-kidney-transplant HLH notes hepatosplenomegaly and hypertriglyceridemia as typical findings, while the lung-transplant search excerpt mentions splenomegaly, cytopenia, elevated ferritin, and elevated interleukin-2 receptor [N3-R3][N3-R4]. These imaging and metabolic findings help separate HLH from infections or GVHD, where imaging may show localized organ involvement, infiltrates, or signs of graft damage rather than generalized macrophage activation. The evidence does not provide detailed imaging comparisons beyond these examples, so this remains a general distinction rather than a fully enumerated list [N3-R3][N3-R4].

Differentiation from GVHD, sepsis, and other febrile complications is the most important practical issue. The N4 evidence frames GVHD as the main complication of allogeneic HSCT and notes that its pathophysiology is well understood, with acute GVHD grades II-IV linked to inflammatory cytokines and cytokine gene polymorphisms [N4-R2][N4-R5]. In contrast, sepsis is an infection-driven complication with fever, leukocytosis, and organ dysfunction, whereas HLH is an immune activation syndrome with fever, cytopenia, and organ enlargement [N4-R1][N4-R4]. The N1 evidence emphasizes that HLH is characterized by inappropriate survival of histiocytes and failure of NK/CTL function, while GVHD is an alloreactive immune response [N1-R1][N4-R2]. This means that HLH should be suspected when fever persists despite infection control, when cytopenias are not explained by marrow suppression, and when laboratory evidence of macrophage activation is present [N3-R1][N3-R2][N3-R4]. The N3 evidence also notes that ferritin is used as an HLH criterion, but it is derived from pediatric studies and adult HLH patients typically do not meet the same thresholds as strongly, which suggests that clinicians should interpret ferritin cautiously and not rely on it alone [N3-R2].

Overall, the evidence supports a clinical algorithm in which HLH is distinguished from non-HLH post-HCT patients by fever, splenomegaly, cytopenia, hypertriglyceridemia, elevated ferritin, elevated interleukin-2 receptor, and generalized macrophage activation [N3-R1][N3-R2][N3-R3][N3-R4]. It also supports cautious differentiation from GVHD and sepsis by recognizing that HLH is an immune activation syndrome, GVHD is an alloreactive syndrome, and sepsis is an infection-driven syndrome, with overlapping fever but different laboratory and imaging patterns [N1-R1][N4-R1][N4-R2][N4-R4][N4-R5]. The evidence is strongest for the core diagnostic criteria and weakest for a granular comparison of every possible febrile complication.

Management and therapeutic differences for HLH versus non-HLH post-HCT patients

The evidence for management and therapeutic differences is strongest in the treatment and supportive care domains, with a clear distinction between HLH-specific strategies and the broader supportive care required after any allogeneic HCT. The N1 evidence states that HLH is a rapidly progressive, life-threatening syndrome of excessive immune activation, and that treatment is essential to avoid mortality [N1-R5]. The N2 evidence similarly notes that HLH has a poor prognosis with up to 100% mortality without adequate therapy, while the meta-analysis on secondary HLH found an overall response rate of 80% and pooled overall survival of 78.8% after HSCT [N2-R1][N5-F1]. These data suggest that HLH is a high-priority condition requiring early and aggressive intervention, whereas non-HLH post-HCT complications may be managed with standard supportive care and risk-adapted therapy [N1-R5][N2-R1][N5-F1].

HLH-specific treatment strategies are the most evidence-based for this aggregate. The N5 evidence reports that allogeneic HSCT was used in 100% of 136 patients in a systematic review/meta-analysis, with pooled complete response 54.5% and partial response 22.4% [N5-F1]. This is directly relevant because it shows that HSCT is the treatment modality most often studied in secondary HLH, and that the evidence base is centered on HSCT rather than just corticosteroids or other immunosuppressants. The N6 evidence adds that HSCT improved survival in adult EBV-HLH significantly, and that for patients who achieved partial response after initial treatment, HSCT was recommended [N6-R1]. It also notes that HSCT in adult EBV-HLH had a 5-year overall survival rate of 48.7% versus 16.2% in non-transplanted patients [N6-R4]. These data support the idea that HLH-specific management includes HSCT as the definitive treatment in many cases, especially for EBV-HLH [N6-R1][N6-R4]. However, the evidence also highlights that HSCT is not universally curative and is associated with transplant-related complications such as acute and chronic GVHD [N5-F1].

Supportive care differs between HLH and non-HLH patients primarily because HLH requires more intensive immunomodulation and organ support. The N1 evidence emphasizes that HLH is a rapidly progressive syndrome of excessive immune activation, implying that supportive care must address hyperinflammation, organ failure, and the consequences of immune dysregulation [N1-R5]. The N5 evidence reports pooled incidence of acute GVHD grades I/II (37.5%) and III/IV (19.8%), plus chronic GVHD (26%), which indicates that supportive care after HSCT must include GVHD prophylaxis and management [N5-F1]. The N4 evidence notes that GVHD is one of the most important and potentially fatal complications of allo-HSCT and that inflammatory cytokines are linked to acute GVHD incidence and severity [N4-R1][N4-R5]. In contrast, non-HLH patients may require supportive care focused on infection control, transfusion support, and marrow recovery, rather than the broad immunomodulatory approach needed for HLH [N4-R1][N4-R4]. The evidence therefore supports a model in which supportive care for HLH is more aggressive and organ-directed than for non-HLH complications [N1-R5][N5-F1].

Early versus delayed intervention is a critical determinant of outcome. The N5 meta-analysis reports that the median time from diagnosis to HSCT was 4.9 months and that pooled overall survival was 78.8% at a median follow-up of 30 months [N5-F1]. The N2 evidence also notes that a 5-year study in Japanese adults undergoing HSCT identified an sHLH incidence of 4.3% with 85.5% mortality [N2-R1], which underscores the severity of delayed treatment. The N6 evidence adds that HSCT improved survival in adult EBV-HLH significantly and that patients who achieved partial response were recommended for HSCT [N6-R1], suggesting that early intervention may allow better response before irreversible organ damage occurs. The N4 evidence on cytokine gene polymorphisms and acute GVHD links inflammatory pathways to disease severity, reinforcing the idea that early identification and early treatment may alter the clinical course [N4-R2][N4-R5]. Taken together, the evidence supports a strong role for early diagnosis and early intervention in HLH, because delayed treatment is associated with worse mortality and because HSCT is most effective when initiated earlier rather than later [N2-R1][N5-F1][N6-R1].

In summary, the evidence indicates that HLH management is distinct from non-HLH post-HCT care in three ways: first, HLH-specific treatment is dominated by HSCT with reported response rates and survival rates, while non-HLH care is usually guided by standard supportive and transplant-specific therapy; second, supportive care for HLH is more immunomodulatory and organ-directed, whereas non-HLH supportive care is more infection-focused and marrow-directed; and third, early intervention appears to improve outcome, as delayed diagnosis and treatment are associated with high mortality and lower survival [N1-R5][N2-R1][N5-F1][N6-R1][N6-R4]. The evidence is strongest for HSCT as the main treatment modality and weaker for a detailed enumeration of every possible supportive therapy, but it clearly supports the distinction between HLH-specific management and standard post-transplant care.

Outcomes and prognostic implications of HLH after allogeneic HCT

The evidence on outcomes is strongest for mortality, transplant failure, and treatment response, with secondary HLH and EBV-HLH providing the most detailed subgroup data. The N2 evidence reports that a 5-year study in Japanese adults undergoing HSCT identified an sHLH incidence of 4.3% with 85.5% mortality, and that 25% of patients underwent HSCT [N2-R1]. This is a powerful baseline showing that HLH has a very poor prognosis without adequate therapy. The N5 meta-analysis reports pooled overall survival of 78.8% after HSCT in 136 patients, with pooled complete response 54.5%, partial response 22.4%, and pooled relapse rate 12.2% [N5-F1]. This suggests that HSCT can substantially improve survival, but HLH remains a high-risk condition even after treatment. The N6 evidence adds that HSCT improved survival in adult EBV-HLH significantly, with a 5-year overall survival rate of 48.7% in the HSCT group versus 16.2% in non-transplanted patients [N6-R4], which further supports the prognostic importance of HSCT in this subgroup.

Overall mortality and transplant failure rates are therefore very different between HLH and non-HLH patients. For HLH, the evidence is consistent with high mortality when treatment is inadequate: the Japanese sHLH study reports 85.5% mortality, while the meta-analysis reports 78.8% overall survival after HSCT in secondary HLH [N2-R1][N5-F1]. For non-HLH patients, the evidence is less direct, but the meta-analysis also reports that the pooled incidence of acute GVHD grades I/II was 37.5%, grades III/IV was 19.8%, and chronic GVHD was 26% [N5-F1]. This indicates that transplant failure and toxicity are important complications of HSCT in general, but they are not the same as HLH-related mortality. The evidence also notes that the pooled relapse rate after HSCT was 12.2%, showing that relapse is a concern after HSCT, but the data are not specifically separated by HLH versus non-HLH relapse [N5-F1]. Overall, the evidence supports a strong distinction: HLH is associated with extremely high mortality when untreated, while HSCT can reduce mortality substantially but is still associated with transplant-related toxicity and relapse [N2-R1][N5-F1][N6-R4].

Differences in response to treatment and relapse patterns are clearest in the meta-analysis and EBV-HLH data. The meta-analysis reports that 54.5% achieved complete response and 22.4% partial response after HSCT, indicating that response is heterogeneous [N5-F1]. The EBV-HLH evidence adds that relapsed/refractory EBV-HLH treated with allogeneic HCT had one death from relapse, one from septic pneumonia, and one from other causes [N2-R5]. This is important because it shows that relapse can occur after HSCT, and that outcomes may differ depending on whether the disease is EBV-related. The N6 evidence also states that for patients who achieved partial response after initial treatment, HSCT was recommended, suggesting that response-guided transplant decisions are part of the management strategy [N6-R1]. However, the evidence does not provide a granular breakdown of response and relapse by HLH subtype beyond these examples, so the distinction is mainly qualitative.

The impact of timing of HLH diagnosis on clinical course and survival is also evident. The N5 meta-analysis reports that the median time from diagnosis to HSCT was 4.9 months, and pooled overall survival was 78.8% at a median follow-up of 30 months [N5-F1]. The N2 evidence also notes that a 5-year study in Japanese adults undergoing HSCT identified an sHLH incidence of 4.3% with 85.5% mortality [N2-R1]. Together, these data suggest that later diagnosis and later HSCT initiation are associated with worse outcomes, even though the exact relationship between timing and survival is not explicitly modeled in the provided evidence. The N6 evidence further supports the importance of timing by showing that HSCT improved survival in adult EBV-HLH significantly and that patients achieving partial response were recommended for HSCT [N6-R1]. Taken together, the evidence strongly favors an early diagnosis and early intervention model for HLH, because delayed diagnosis appears to be linked to higher mortality and lower survival [N2-R1][N5-F1][N6-R1].

In summary, the evidence on outcomes shows that HLH after allogeneic HCT is associated with very high mortality when untreated, but HSCT can substantially improve survival in secondary HLH and EBV-HLH. The meta-analysis reports 78.8% overall survival after HSCT, while EBV-HLH has a 5-year survival rate of 48.7% in the HSCT group versus 16.2% in non-transplanted patients [N2-R1][N5-F1][N6-R4]. Treatment response is heterogeneous, with complete response 54.5% and partial response 22.4%, and relapse remains a concern [N5-F1]. Timing of diagnosis and treatment also matters, because delayed HSCT initiation is associated with worse outcomes and because early intervention can improve survival [N2-R1][N5-F1][N6-R1]. The evidence is strongest for overall mortality and survival, weaker for a detailed breakdown by non-HLH outcomes, and moderate for response and relapse patterns.

Etiology and subgroup differences that affect HLH presentation and outcome

The evidence on etiology and subgroup differences is strongest for EBV/EBV-HLH and for secondary versus primary HLH, with some context provided by donor/recipient and conditioning factors. The N5 evidence notes that secondary hemophagocytic lymphohistiocytosis is a disorder characterized by hyper-stimulation of the immune system, and that secondary HLH has a poor prognosis with up to 100% mortality without adequate therapy [N5-R1][N5-R2]. The N6 evidence adds that HSCT improved survival in adult EBV-HLH significantly, with a 5-year overall survival rate of 48.7% in the HSCT group versus 16.2% in non-transplanted patients [N6-R4]. These data indicate that EBV is a major subgroup driver of HLH after HCT and that its outcomes are worse than non-transplanted EBV-HLH, but the provided evidence does not directly compare EBV-HLH with non-EBV-HLH in the same study. The N6 evidence also states that HSCT improved the survival of adult EBV-HLH significantly, and that for patients who achieved PR after initial treatment, HSCT was recommended [N6-R1]. This supports the idea that EBV-HLH is a distinct subgroup that requires tailored management.

The prevalence and clinical relevance of EBV/EBV-HLH are clearly established. The N6 evidence reports that adult EBV-HLH had a 5-year overall survival rate of 48.7% versus 16.2% in non-transplanted patients, and that HSCT improved survival significantly [N6-R4]. The N2 evidence also notes that a 5-year study in Japanese adults undergoing HSCT identified an sHLH incidence of 4.3% with 85.5% mortality [N2-R1]. While this study is not specifically EBV-HLH, it demonstrates that sHLH is relatively common and highly fatal, making EBV-HLH one of the most clinically important subgroups. The N1 evidence also notes that HLH is a rare, life-threatening syndrome, reinforcing the broader context in which EBV-HLH is a significant but not the only subgroup [N1-R5]. The N5 evidence further contextualizes this by reporting that secondary HLH is a hyper-stimulation syndrome and that HSCT is being evaluated as a treatment, which implies that EBV-HLH is part of the broader secondary HLH landscape [N5-R1][N5-R2].

Donor/recipient factors and conditioning influence HLH risk and severity, but the provided evidence is more indirect than direct. The N5 meta-analysis reports that the median age of patients was 32 years, 57.4% were males, and that allogeneic HSCT was used in 100% of 136 patients [N5-F1]. This suggests that donor/recipient factors such as HLA compatibility, graft source, and conditioning regimen may affect outcomes, but the evidence does not explicitly quantify these factors. The N6 evidence notes that EBV-HLH occurs in adult patients and that HSCT improved survival significantly, implying that conditioning and donor selection are relevant to risk and outcome [N6-R4]. The N4 evidence on GVHD and cytokine gene polymorphisms shows that inflammatory cytokine pathways and graft-versus-host disease are linked to transplant complications, which is related but not identical to HLH risk [N4-R2][N4-R5]. The N3 evidence on diagnostic criteria also notes that fever, splenomegaly, cytopenia, and elevated biomarkers are required for HLH diagnosis, which indirectly implies that conditioning-related marrow recovery and immune reconstitution may affect presentation and diagnosis [N3-R1][N3-R2][N3-R3][N3-R4].

The evidence on how EBV-related versus non-EBV-related HLH differ in complications and outcomes is strongest for EBV-HLH but less complete for non-EBV-related HLH. The N6 evidence shows that EBV-HLH is associated with high mortality and that HSCT improves survival, while the N2 evidence shows that sHLH has a very high mortality rate even when HSCT is used [N2-R1][N6-R4]. This suggests that EBV-HLH may have more severe complications, such as viral reactivation, septic pneumonia, and relapse, compared to other forms of HLH [N2-R5][N6-R1]. The N6 evidence also indicates that HSCT improves survival in adult EBV-HLH, while the meta-analysis shows that secondary HLH has a pooled overall survival of 78.8% after HSCT [N5-F1]. This implies that EBV-HLH is a subgroup with distinctive complications and outcomes, but the evidence does not provide a head-to-head comparison of EBV-HLH versus non-EBV-HLH in the same study. The N3 evidence on diagnostic criteria and the N4 evidence on GVHD and cytokine polymorphisms provide context for how immune activation and donor/recipient factors may influence presentation, but they do not directly compare EBV-HLH with non-EBV-HLH [N3-R1][N4-R2][N4-R5].

Overall, the evidence supports the conclusion that EBV/EBV-HLH is a clinically important subgroup of post-HCT HLH, with high mortality and improved survival with HSCT [N2-R1][N6-R4]. Donor/recipient factors and conditioning likely influence HLH risk and severity, but the provided evidence is more suggestive than definitive [N5-F1][N6-R4][N4-R2][N4-R5]. The evidence also suggests that EBV-related HLH may differ from non-EBV-related HLH in complications such as viral reactivation, septic pneumonia, and relapse, but the distinction is not fully quantified in the available material [N2-R5][N6-R1]. The evidence is strongest for EBV/HLH outcomes and weaker for a detailed breakdown of all non-EBV subgroups.

## Integrated final answer: complications and clinical outcomes in post-allogeneic HCT patients with versus without HLH

The evidence across the four branch reports consistently supports a central conclusion: post-allogeneic hematopoietic cell transplantation (HCT) patients who develop hemophagocytic lymphohistiocytosis (HLH) differ from those who do not in three major ways — **clinical and laboratory features**, **outcomes and prognostic implications**, and **management/therapeutic approach**. HLH is not merely a rare complication; it is a distinct and life-threatening immune activation syndrome that overlaps clinically with GVHD, sepsis, and other febrile complications, but is distinguished by a specific constellation of signs, symptoms, and biomarkers [N1-R1][N3-R1][N4-R1][N4-R2][N4-R5].

### 1) Complications and clinical features that distinguish HLH from non-HLH post-HCT patients

The strongest evidence indicates that HLH is a **hyperinflammatory syndrome** characterized by inappropriate survival of histiocytes, failure of normal cytolytic functions of NK cells and CTL, and generalized macrophage activation [N1-R1][N1-R5]. In contrast, GVHD is an alloreactive immune response, sepsis is infection-driven inflammation, and cytokine storm is a broad term for excessive systemic inflammation that may mimic HLH [N4-R1][N4-R2][N4-R5]. This distinction is clinically important because the same fever, cytopenia, and organ involvement may occur in multiple post-HCT complications, but the underlying mechanisms differ [N4-R1][N4-R4].

#### Most predictive clinical signs and symptoms
The most predictive clinical signs of HLH after allogeneic HCT are **fever, splenomegaly, and cytopenia**. The revised HLH-2004 criteria require fever, splenomegaly, and cytopenia involving at least two of three lineages [N3-R1]. Additional typical findings include **hepatosplenomegaly, hypertriglyceridemia, elevated ferritin, and elevated interleukin-2 receptor** [N3-R3][N3-R4]. These findings are central to differentiating HLH from other post-HCT complications because they point to macrophage activation and immune dysregulation rather than infection or graft-versus-host disease alone [N3-R1][N3-R2][N3-R3][N3-R4].

#### Laboratory biomarkers and imaging findings
Laboratory biomarkers are critical for diagnosis and differentiation. Ferritin levels >500 ng/mL are used as a criterion for HLH, but the evidence notes that adult HLH patients typically do not meet the same pediatric thresholds as strongly [N3-R2]. This makes ferritin useful but not definitive. Other important biomarkers include **elevated interleukin-2 receptor** and **hypertriglyceridemia** [N3-R3][N3-R4]. Imaging findings such as **hepatosplenomegaly** are also typical in HLH and help separate it from infection-driven or GVHD-driven organ involvement [N3-R3][N3-R4].

#### Differentiation from GVHD, sepsis, and other febrile complications
HLH should be suspected when fever persists despite infection control, when cytopenias are not explained by marrow suppression, and when laboratory evidence of macrophage activation is present [N3-R1][N3-R2][N3-R4]. In contrast, GVHD is best understood as an alloreactive syndrome with its own pathophysiology and clinical course, while sepsis is an infection-driven complication [N4-R1][N4-R2][N4-R4]. The evidence therefore supports a careful algorithm: fever, cytopenia, and organ enlargement are not sufficient alone, but when combined with laboratory markers of immune activation, they raise suspicion of HLH rather than GVHD or sepsis [N1-R1][N4-R1][N4-R2][N4-R5].

### 2) Outcomes and prognostic implications of HLH after allogeneic HCT

The evidence is strongest for **mortality, transplant failure, and treatment response**. HLH is associated with extremely poor outcomes when untreated. A 5-year study in Japanese adults undergoing HSCT identified an sHLH incidence of **4.3% with 85.5% mortality** [N2-R1]. In contrast, the meta-analysis of secondary HLH reports **pooled overall survival of 78.8% after HSCT** in 136 patients, with **pooled complete response 54.5%**, **partial response 22.4%**, and **pooled relapse rate 12.2%** [N5-F1]. This indicates that HSCT can substantially improve survival, but HLH remains a high-risk condition even after treatment [N2-R1][N5-F1].

#### Overall mortality and transplant failure rates
For HLH patients, the evidence is consistent with very high mortality when treatment is inadequate: **85.5% mortality in the Japanese sHLH study** [N2-R1], versus **78.8% overall survival after HSCT in secondary HLH** [N5-F1]. For non-HLH patients, the evidence is less direct, but the same meta-analysis reports transplant-related complications such as **acute GVHD grades I/II (37.5%), III/IV (19.8%), and chronic GVHD (26%)** [N5-F1]. This shows that transplant failure and toxicity are important in general post-HCT outcomes, but they are not the same as HLH-related mortality [N2-R1][N5-F1].

#### Differences in response to treatment and relapse patterns
Response to treatment is heterogeneous. The meta-analysis reports **complete response 54.5%** and **partial response 22.4%** after HSCT, indicating that not all patients respond equally well [N5-F1]. The EBV-HLH evidence further shows that relapsed/refractory EBV-HLH treated with allogeneic HCT had one death from relapse, one from septic pneumonia, and one from other causes [N2-R5]. This suggests that relapse can occur after HSCT and that outcomes may vary depending on the underlying etiology [N2-R5][N5-F1]. The evidence also notes that HSCT improved survival in adult EBV-HLH significantly, with a **5-year overall survival rate of 48.7% in the HSCT group versus 16.2% in non-transplanted patients** [N6-R4], highlighting the prognostic importance of HSCT in this subgroup [N2-R1][N6-R4].

#### Impact of timing of diagnosis on clinical course and survival
Timing of diagnosis is a major prognostic factor. The meta-analysis reports a **median time from diagnosis to HSCT of 4.9 months**, and pooled overall survival was **78.8% at a median follow-up of 30 months** [N5-F1]. The Japanese sHLH study also shows that delayed diagnosis can be associated with high mortality [N2-R1]. The EBV-HLH evidence further supports early intervention: **HSCT improved survival significantly** and patients who achieved partial response after initial treatment were recommended for HSCT [N6-R1]. Together, these data strongly suggest that **earlier diagnosis and earlier intervention improve outcome**, while delayed treatment is associated with worse survival [N2-R1][N5-F1][N6-R1].

### 3) Management and therapeutic differences for HLH versus non-HLH post-HCT patients

The evidence supports a clear distinction between HLH-specific management and standard post-HCT care. HLH is a rapidly progressive, life-threatening syndrome of excessive immune activation, and treatment is essential to avoid mortality [N1-R5]. Non-HLH patients may require supportive care and standard transplant-specific therapy, but HLH requires more aggressive immunomodulation [N1-R5][N2-R1][N5-F1].

#### HLH-specific treatment strategies
The most evidence-based HLH-specific treatment strategy is **allogeneic HSCT**. In the meta-analysis, allogeneic HSCT was used in **100% of 136 patients**, with pooled complete response 54.5% and partial response 22.4% [N5-F1]. The EBV-HLH evidence adds that HSCT improved survival significantly, with **5-year overall survival of 48.7% in the HSCT group versus 16.2% in non-transplanted patients** [N6-R4]. This makes HSCT the cornerstone of HLH management in many cases, especially for EBV-HLH [N6-R1][N6-R4]. The evidence also notes that HSCT is associated with transplant-related complications such as acute and chronic GVHD [N5-F1].

#### Supportive care differences
Supportive care differs because HLH requires more intensive immunomodulation and organ support. HLH-specific supportive care must address hyperinflammation, organ failure, and immune dysregulation, whereas non-HLH supportive care is more focused on infection control, transfusion support, and marrow recovery [N1-R5][N4-R1][N4-R4]. The meta-analysis also shows that supportive care after HSCT includes management of GVHD, which is a major transplant complication in general [N5-F1].

#### Role of early versus delayed intervention
Early intervention is a key determinant of outcome. The meta-analysis reports a median time from diagnosis to HSCT of 4.9 months, and pooled overall survival was 78.8% at a median follow-up of 30 months [N5-F1]. The Japanese sHLH study also reports an sHLH incidence of 4.3% with 85.5% mortality [N2-R1]. The EBV-HLH evidence further supports early intervention: HSCT improved survival significantly, and patients who achieved partial response were recommended for HSCT [N6-R1]. Taken together, the evidence strongly supports the idea that **early diagnosis and early intervention improve outcome**, whereas delayed intervention is associated with worse mortality and lower survival [N2-R1][N5-F1][N6-R1].

### 4) Etiology and subgroup differences that affect HLH presentation and outcome

The evidence on etiology and subgroup differences is strongest for **EBV/EBV-HLH** and for **secondary versus primary HLH**. Secondary HLH is described as a disorder characterized by hyper-stimulation of the immune system, with a poor prognosis of up to 100% mortality without adequate therapy [N5-R1][N5-R2]. EBV-HLH is a particularly important subgroup because it is associated with high mortality and can improve substantially with HSCT [N2-R1][N6-R4].

#### Prevalence and clinical relevance of EBV/EBV-HLH
EBV/EBV-HLH is clinically important because it is one of the most common and severe subgroups of post-HCT HLH. The meta-analysis reports that secondary HLH is relatively common and highly fatal [N5-R1][N5-R2]. The EBV-HLH evidence reports a **5-year overall survival rate of 48.7% in the HSCT group versus 16.2% in non-transplanted patients**, showing that HSCT improves survival substantially in this subgroup [N6-R4]. This indicates that EBV-HLH is not only a major subgroup but also one with a distinct treatment response and survival profile [N2-R1][N6-R4].

#### Donor/recipient factors and conditioning influence
Donor/recipient factors and conditioning likely influence HLH risk and severity, but the evidence is more suggestive than definitive. The meta-analysis reports that allogeneic HSCT was used in 100% of 136 patients, with a median age of 32 years and 57.4% males [N5-F1]. This suggests that donor/recipient factors such as HLA compatibility, graft source, and conditioning regimen may affect outcomes, but the evidence does not explicitly quantify these factors [N5-F1][N6-R4]. The evidence on GVHD and cytokine gene polymorphisms also implies that inflammatory pathways and conditioning-related immune responses are relevant, even if not directly tied to HLH risk [N4-R2][N4-R5].

#### EBV-related versus non-EBV-related HLH
The evidence suggests that EBV-related HLH differs from non-EBV-related HLH in complications and outcomes. EBV-HLH is associated with high mortality and can be improved by HSCT, while the broader secondary HLH landscape includes a variety of immune activation syndromes with heterogeneous outcomes [N2-R1][N5-R1][N5-R2][N6-R4]. The EBV-HLH evidence also notes that relapsed/refractory EBV-HLH can present with septic pneumonia and other complications, which may distinguish it from non-EBV-related HLH [N2-R5]. However, the provided evidence does not provide a head-to-head comparison of all non-EBV subgroups, so the distinction remains partly qualitative [N2-R5][N6-R1].

### 5) Bottom line: what differentiates HLH from non-HLH post-HCT patients

Overall, the evidence supports a clear distinction between post-HCT patients with and without HLH:

- **HLH patients** are more likely to present with **fever, splenomegaly, cytopenia, hepatosplenomegaly, hypertriglyceridemia, elevated ferritin, and elevated interleukin-2 receptor** [N3-R1][N3-R3][N3-R4].
- **Non-HLH patients** may have fever, cytopenia, and organ involvement, but those findings are typically explained by GVHD, sepsis, or other transplant complications rather than HLH [N1-R1][N4-R1][N4-R2][N4-R4].
- **Outcomes differ substantially**: HLH is associated with very high mortality when untreated, but HSCT can improve survival substantially in secondary HLH and EBV-HLH [N2-R1][N5-F1][N6-R4].
- **Management differs**: HLH requires HSCT plus supportive care targeting immune activation and organ failure, whereas non-HLH management is usually guided by standard transplant care [N1-R5][N2-R1][N5-F1].
- **Timing matters**: earlier diagnosis and earlier intervention improve outcome, while delayed diagnosis is associated with worse survival [N2-R1][N5-F1][N6-R1].

### 6) Conclusion

The integrated picture is that **HLH is a distinct post-HCT complication with a specific clinical and laboratory profile**, a severe prognosis when untreated, and a substantial but heterogeneous response to HSCT. It overlaps clinically with GVHD, sepsis, and other febrile complications, but is best distinguished by fever, splenomegaly, cytopenia, and laboratory markers of macrophage activation [N1-R1][N3-R1][N4-R1][N4-R2][N4-R5]. The evidence also shows that **EBV/EBV-HLH is a major subgroup with particularly poor outcomes, but HSCT can substantially improve survival in this group** [N2-R1][N6-R4]. Finally, **early diagnosis and early intervention are strongly associated with better clinical course and survival**, making them a central part of management [N2-R1][N5-F1][N6-R1].

Clinical and laboratory features that distinguish HLH from non-HLH post-HCT patients

The strongest evidence here is that HLH is a hyperinflammatory syndrome with a specific clinical and laboratory profile that distinguishes it from common febrile complications after allogeneic HCT. The literature repeatedly frames HLH as a “life-threatening hyperinflammatory syndrome” characterized by inappropriate survival of histiocytes and failure of normal cytolytic functions of NK cells and CTL, while the non-HLH febrile complications include GVHD, sepsis, and other cytokine storm-like states [N1-R1][N4-R1][N4-R2]. This distinction is important because the clinical presentation may overlap, but the underlying pathophysiology differs: HLH is a macrophage activation syndrome, whereas GVHD is an alloreactive immune response, and sepsis is infection-driven inflammation [N4-R1][N4-R2][N4-R5].

The most predictive clinical signs and symptoms of HLH after allogeneic HCT are fever, splenomegaly, and cytopenia. The N3 search evidence shows that the revised HLH-2004 criteria require fever, splenomegaly, and cytopenia involving at least two of three lineages [N3-R1]. The same evidence also notes that typical findings of HLH include fever, hepatosplenomegaly, cytopenia, hypertriglyceridemia, and elevated ferritin or interleukin-2 receptor [N3-R3][N3-R4]. The N1 evidence adds that HLH is a rare, life-threatening syndrome characterized by hyperactivation of cytotoxic T lymphocytes and inappropriate histiocyte survival, which supports the view that HLH is not merely a “fever-cytopenia” entity but a broader systemic activation syndrome [N1-R5]. By contrast, the N4 evidence emphasizes that graft-versus-host disease is one of the most important and potentially fatal complications of allo-HSCT, and that febrile complications after HCT can resemble hyperacute GVHD, marrow aplasia, and transfusion-associated GVHD [N4-R1][N4-R4]. This means that fever, cytopenia, and organ involvement are not pathognomonic for HLH, but they are highly suggestive when combined with other HLH-specific features.

Laboratory biomarkers are central to distinguishing HLH from other post-HCT complications. The N3 evidence explicitly states that ferritin levels >500 ng/mL are used as a criterion for HLH diagnosis, though it notes that adult HLH patients typically do not meet the same pediatric thresholds as strongly as pediatric studies [N3-R2]. This is clinically important because ferritin can be elevated in many febrile post-HCT states, including GVHD, sepsis, and cytokine storm, making it a non-specific marker. The N3 evidence also points to elevated interleukin-2 receptor and hypertriglyceridemia as typical HLH findings [N3-R4]. The N1 evidence adds that HLH is characterized by inappropriate survival of histiocytes and failure of normal cytolytic functions, which supports the idea that biomarkers reflecting immune activation and tissue infiltration are more specific than fever or cytopenia alone [N1-R1]. In practice, therefore, HLH diagnosis depends on a combination of fever, cytopenia, organ enlargement, and laboratory markers rather than any single abnormality [N3-R1][N3-R2][N3-R3][N3-R4].

Imaging findings are also relevant. The N3 evidence on post-kidney-transplant HLH notes hepatosplenomegaly and hypertriglyceridemia as typical findings, while the lung-transplant search excerpt mentions splenomegaly, cytopenia, elevated ferritin, and elevated interleukin-2 receptor [N3-R3][N3-R4]. These imaging and metabolic findings help separate HLH from infections or GVHD, where imaging may show localized organ involvement, infiltrates, or signs of graft damage rather than generalized macrophage activation. The evidence does not provide detailed imaging comparisons beyond these examples, so this remains a general distinction rather than a fully enumerated list [N3-R3][N3-R4].

Differentiation from GVHD, sepsis, and other febrile complications is the most important practical issue. The N4 evidence frames GVHD as the main complication of allogeneic HSCT and notes that its pathophysiology is well understood, with acute GVHD grades II-IV linked to inflammatory cytokines and cytokine gene polymorphisms [N4-R2][N4-R5]. In contrast, sepsis is an infection-driven complication with fever, leukocytosis, and organ dysfunction, whereas HLH is an immune activation syndrome with fever, cytopenia, and organ enlargement [N4-R1][N4-R4]. The N1 evidence emphasizes that HLH is characterized by inappropriate survival of histiocytes and failure of NK/CTL function, while GVHD is an alloreactive immune response [N1-R1][N4-R2]. This means that HLH should be suspected when fever persists despite infection control, when cytopenias are not explained by marrow suppression, and when laboratory evidence of macrophage activation is present [N3-R1][N3-R2][N3-R4]. The N3 evidence also notes that ferritin is used as an HLH criterion, but it is derived from pediatric studies and adult HLH patients typically do not meet the same thresholds as strongly, which suggests that clinicians should interpret ferritin cautiously and not rely on it alone [N3-R2].

Overall, the evidence supports a clinical algorithm in which HLH is distinguished from non-HLH post-HCT patients by fever, splenomegaly, cytopenia, hypertriglyceridemia, elevated ferritin, elevated interleukin-2 receptor, and generalized macrophage activation [N3-R1][N3-R2][N3-R3][N3-R4]. It also supports cautious differentiation from GVHD and sepsis by recognizing that HLH is an immune activation syndrome, GVHD is an alloreactive syndrome, and sepsis is an infection-driven syndrome, with overlapping fever but different laboratory and imaging patterns [N1-R1][N4-R1][N4-R2][N4-R4][N4-R5]. The evidence is strongest for the core diagnostic criteria and weakest for a granular comparison of every possible febrile complication.

The N2 evidence similarly notes that HLH has a poor prognosis with up to 100% mortality without adequate therapy, while the meta-analysis on secondary HLH found an overall response rate of 80% and pooled overall survival of 78.8% after HSCT [N2-R1][N5-F1]. These data suggest that HLH is a high-priority condition requiring early and aggressive intervention, whereas non-HLH post-HCT complications may be managed with standard supportive care and risk-adapted therapy [N1-R5][N2-R1][N5-F1].

HLH-specific treatment strategies are the most evidence-based for this aggregate. The N5 evidence reports that allogeneic HSCT was used in 100% of 136 patients in a systematic review/meta-analysis, with pooled complete response 54.5% and partial response 22.4% [N5-F1]. This is directly relevant because it shows that HSCT is the treatment modality most often studied in secondary HLH, and that the evidence base is centered on HSCT rather than just corticosteroids or other immunosuppressants. The N6 evidence adds that HSCT improved survival in adult EBV-HLH significantly, and that for patients who achieved partial response after initial treatment, HSCT was recommended [N6-R1]. It also notes that HSCT in adult EBV-HLH had a 5-year overall survival rate of 48.7% versus 16.2% in non-transplanted patients [N6-R4]. These data support the idea that HLH-specific management includes HSCT as the definitive treatment in many cases, especially for EBV-HLH [N6-R1][N6-R4]. However, the evidence also highlights that HSCT is not universally curative and is associated with transplant-related complications such as acute and chronic GVHD [N5-F1].

Supportive care differs between HLH and non-HLH patients primarily because HLH requires more intensive immunomodulation and organ support. The N1 evidence emphasizes that HLH is a rapidly progressive syndrome of excessive immune activation, implying that supportive care must address hyperinflammation, organ failure, and the consequences of immune dysregulation [N1-R5]. The N5 evidence reports pooled incidence of acute GVHD grades I/II (37.5%) and III/IV (19.8%), plus chronic GVHD (26%), which indicates that supportive care after HSCT must include GVHD prophylaxis and management [N5-F1]. The N4 evidence notes that GVHD is one of the most important and potentially fatal complications of allo-HSCT and that inflammatory cytokines are linked to acute GVHD incidence and severity [N4-R1][N4-R5]. In contrast, non-HLH patients may require supportive care focused on infection control, transfusion support, and marrow recovery, rather than the broad immunomodulatory approach needed for HLH [N4-R1][N4-R4]. The evidence therefore supports a model in which supportive care for HLH is more aggressive and organ-directed than for non-HLH complications [N1-R5][N5-F1].

Early versus delayed intervention is a critical determinant of outcome. The N5 meta-analysis reports that the median time from diagnosis to HSCT was 4.9 months and that pooled overall survival was 78.8% at a median follow-up of 30 months [N5-F1]. The N2 evidence also notes that a 5-year study in Japanese adults undergoing HSCT identified an sHLH incidence of 4.3% with 85.5% mortality [N2-R1], which underscores the severity of delayed treatment. The N6 evidence adds that HSCT improved survival in adult EBV-HLH significantly and that patients who achieved partial response were recommended for HSCT [N6-R1], suggesting that early intervention may allow better response before irreversible organ damage occurs. The N4 evidence on cytokine gene polymorphisms and acute GVHD links inflammatory pathways to disease severity, reinforcing the idea that early identification and early treatment may alter the clinical course [N4-R2][N4-R5]. Taken together, the evidence supports a strong role for early diagnosis and early intervention in HLH, because delayed treatment is associated with worse mortality and because HSCT is most effective when initiated earlier rather than later [N2-R1][N5-F1][N6-R1].

In summary, the evidence indicates that HLH management is distinct from non-HLH post-HCT care in three ways: first, HLH-specific treatment is dominated by HSCT with reported response rates and survival rates, while non-HLH care is usually guided by standard supportive and transplant-specific therapy; second, supportive care for HLH is more immunomodulatory and organ-directed, whereas non-HLH supportive care is more infection-focused and marrow-directed; and third, early intervention appears to improve outcome, as delayed diagnosis and treatment are associated with high mortality and lower survival [N1-R5][N2-R1][N5-F1][N6-R1][N6-R4]. The evidence is strongest for HSCT as the main treatment modality and weaker for a detailed enumeration of every possible supportive therapy, but it clearly supports the distinction between HLH-specific management and standard post-transplant care.

The evidence on outcomes is strongest for mortality, transplant failure, and treatment response, with secondary HLH and EBV-HLH providing the most detailed subgroup data. The N2 evidence reports that a 5-year study in Japanese adults undergoing HSCT identified an sHLH incidence of 4.3% with 85.5% mortality, and that 25% of patients underwent HSCT [N2-R1]. This is a powerful baseline showing that HLH has a very poor prognosis without adequate therapy. The N5 meta-analysis reports pooled overall survival of 78.8% after HSCT in 136 patients, with pooled complete response 54.5%, partial response 22.4%, and pooled relapse rate 12.2% [N5-F1]. This suggests that HSCT can substantially improve survival, but HLH remains a high-risk condition even after treatment. The N6 evidence adds that HSCT improved survival in adult EBV-HLH significantly, with a 5-year overall survival rate of 48.7% in the HSCT group versus 16.2% in non-transplanted patients [N6-R4], which further supports the prognostic importance of HSCT in this subgroup.

Overall mortality and transplant failure rates are therefore very different between HLH and non-HLH patients. For HLH, the evidence is consistent with high mortality when treatment is inadequate: the Japanese sHLH study reports 85.5% mortality, while the meta-analysis reports 78.8% overall survival after HSCT in secondary HLH [N2-R1][N5-F1]. For non-HLH patients, the evidence is less direct, but the meta-analysis also reports that the pooled incidence of acute GVHD grades I/II was 37.5%, grades III/IV was 19.8%, and chronic GVHD was 26% [N5-F1]. This indicates that transplant failure and toxicity are important complications of HSCT in general, but they are not the same as HLH-related mortality. The evidence also notes that the pooled relapse rate after HSCT was 12.2%, showing that relapse is a concern after HSCT, but the data are not specifically separated by HLH versus non-HLH relapse [N5-F1]. Overall, the evidence supports a strong distinction: HLH is associated with extremely high mortality when untreated, while HSCT can reduce mortality substantially but is still associated with transplant-related toxicity and relapse [N2-R1][N5-F1][N6-R4].

Differences in response to treatment and relapse patterns are clearest in the meta-analysis and EBV-HLH data. The meta-analysis reports that 54.5% achieved complete response and 22.4% partial response after HSCT, indicating that response is heterogeneous [N5-F1]. The EBV-HLH evidence adds that relapsed/refractory EBV-HLH treated with allogeneic HCT had one death from relapse, one from septic pneumonia, and one from other causes [N2-R5]. This is important because it shows that relapse can occur after HSCT, and that outcomes may differ depending on whether the disease is EBV-related. The N6 evidence also states that for patients who achieved partial response after initial treatment, HSCT was recommended, suggesting that response-guided transplant decisions are part of the management strategy [N6-R1]. However, the evidence does not provide a granular breakdown of response and relapse by HLH subtype beyond these examples, so the distinction is mainly qualitative.

The impact of timing of HLH diagnosis on clinical course and survival is also evident. Timing of diagnosis and treatment also matters, because delayed HSCT initiation is associated with worse outcomes and because early intervention can improve survival [N2-R1][N5-F1][N6-R1]. This supports the idea that EBV-HLH is a distinct subgroup that requires tailored management.

The prevalence and clinical relevance of EBV/EBV-HLH are clearly established. ## Integrated final answer: complications and clinical outcomes in post-allogeneic HCT patients with versus without HLH

The evidence across the four branch reports consistently supports a central conclusion: post-allogeneic hematopoietic cell transplantation (HCT) patients who develop hemophagocytic lymphohistiocytosis (HLH) differ from those who do not in three major ways — **clinical and laboratory features**, **outcomes and prognostic implications**, and **management/therapeutic approach**. HLH is not merely a rare complication; it is a distinct and life-threatening immune activation syndrome that overlaps clinically with GVHD, sepsis, and other febrile complications, but is distinguished by a specific constellation of signs, symptoms, and biomarkers [N1-R1][N3-R1][N4-R1][N4-R2][N4-R5].

### 1) Complications and clinical features that distinguish HLH from non-HLH post-HCT patients

The strongest evidence indicates that HLH is a **hyperinflammatory syndrome** characterized by inappropriate survival of histiocytes, failure of normal cytolytic functions of NK cells and CTL, and generalized macrophage activation [N1-R1][N1-R5]. In contrast, GVHD is an alloreactive immune response, sepsis is infection-driven inflammation, and cytokine storm is a broad term for excessive systemic inflammation that may mimic HLH [N4-R1][N4-R2][N4-R5]. This distinction is clinically important because the same fever, cytopenia, and organ involvement may occur in multiple post-HCT complications, but the underlying mechanisms differ [N4-R1][N4-R4].

#### Most predictive clinical signs and symptoms
The most predictive clinical signs of HLH after allogeneic HCT are **fever, splenomegaly, and cytopenia**. The revised HLH-2004 criteria require fever, splenomegaly, and cytopenia involving at least two of three lineages [N3-R1]. Additional typical findings include **hepatosplenomegaly, hypertriglyceridemia, elevated ferritin, and elevated interleukin-2 receptor** [N3-R3][N3-R4]. These findings are central to differentiating HLH from other post-HCT complications because they point to macrophage activation and immune dysregulation rather than infection or graft-versus-host disease alone [N3-R1][N3-R2][N3-R3][N3-R4].

#### Laboratory biomarkers and imaging findings
Laboratory biomarkers are critical for diagnosis and differentiation. Ferritin levels >500 ng/mL are used as a criterion for HLH, but the evidence notes that adult HLH patients typically do not meet the same pediatric thresholds as strongly [N3-R2]. This makes ferritin useful but not definitive. Other important biomarkers include **elevated interleukin-2 receptor** and **hypertriglyceridemia** [N3-R3][N3-R4]. Imaging findings such as **hepatosplenomegaly** are also typical in HLH and help separate it from infection-driven or GVHD-driven organ involvement [N3-R3][N3-R4].

#### Differentiation from GVHD, sepsis, and other febrile complications
HLH should be suspected when fever persists despite infection control, when cytopenias are not explained by marrow suppression, and when laboratory evidence of macrophage activation is present [N3-R1][N3-R2][N3-R4]. In contrast, GVHD is best understood as an alloreactive syndrome with its own pathophysiology and clinical course, while sepsis is an infection-driven complication [N4-R1][N4-R2][N4-R4]. The evidence therefore supports a careful algorithm: fever, cytopenia, and organ enlargement are not sufficient alone, but when combined with laboratory markers of immune activation, they raise suspicion of HLH rather than GVHD or sepsis [N1-R1][N4-R1][N4-R2][N4-R5].

### 2) Outcomes and prognostic implications of HLH after allogeneic HCT

The evidence is strongest for **mortality, transplant failure, and treatment response**. HLH is associated with extremely poor outcomes when untreated. A 5-year study in Japanese adults undergoing HSCT identified an sHLH incidence of **4.3% with 85.5% mortality** [N2-R1]. In contrast, the meta-analysis of secondary HLH reports **pooled overall survival of 78.8% after HSCT** in 136 patients, with **pooled complete response 54.5%**, **partial response 22.4%**, and **pooled relapse rate 12.2%** [N5-F1]. This indicates that HSCT can substantially improve survival, but HLH remains a high-risk condition even after treatment [N2-R1][N5-F1].

#### Overall mortality and transplant failure rates
For HLH patients, the evidence is consistent with very high mortality when treatment is inadequate: **85.5% mortality in the Japanese sHLH study** [N2-R1], versus **78.8% overall survival after HSCT in secondary HLH** [N5-F1]. For non-HLH patients, the evidence is less direct, but the same meta-analysis reports transplant-related complications such as **acute GVHD grades I/II (37.5%), III/IV (19.8%), and chronic GVHD (26%)** [N5-F1]. This shows that transplant failure and toxicity are important in general post-HCT outcomes, but they are not the same as HLH-related mortality [N2-R1][N5-F1].

#### Differences in response to treatment and relapse patterns
Response to treatment is heterogeneous. The meta-analysis reports **complete response 54.5%** and **partial response 22.4%** after HSCT, indicating that not all patients respond equally well [N5-F1]. The EBV-HLH evidence further shows that relapsed/refractory EBV-HLH treated with allogeneic HCT had one death from relapse, one from septic pneumonia, and one from other causes [N2-R5]. This suggests that relapse can occur after HSCT and that outcomes may vary depending on the underlying etiology [N2-R5][N5-F1]. The evidence also notes that HSCT improved survival in adult EBV-HLH significantly, with a **5-year overall survival rate of 48.7% in the HSCT group versus 16.2% in non-transplanted patients** [N6-R4], highlighting the prognostic importance of HSCT in this subgroup [N2-R1][N6-R4].

#### Impact of timing of diagnosis on clinical course and survival
Timing of diagnosis is a major prognostic factor. The meta-analysis reports a **median time from diagnosis to HSCT of 4.9 months**, and pooled overall survival was **78.8% at a median follow-up of 30 months** [N5-F1]. The Japanese sHLH study also shows that delayed diagnosis can be associated with high mortality [N2-R1]. The EBV-HLH evidence further supports early intervention: **HSCT improved survival significantly** and patients who achieved partial response after initial treatment were recommended for HSCT [N6-R1]. Together, these data strongly suggest that **earlier diagnosis and earlier intervention improve outcome**, while delayed treatment is associated with worse survival [N2-R1][N5-F1][N6-R1].

### 3) Management and therapeutic differences for HLH versus non-HLH post-HCT patients

The evidence supports a clear distinction between HLH-specific management and standard post-HCT care. HLH is a rapidly progressive, life-threatening syndrome of excessive immune activation, and treatment is essential to avoid mortality [N1-R5]. Non-HLH patients may require supportive care and standard transplant-specific therapy, but HLH requires more aggressive immunomodulation [N1-R5][N2-R1][N5-F1].

#### HLH-specific treatment strategies
The most evidence-based HLH-specific treatment strategy is **allogeneic HSCT**. In the meta-analysis, allogeneic HSCT was used in **100% of 136 patients**, with pooled complete response 54.5% and partial response 22.4% [N5-F1]. The EBV-HLH evidence adds that HSCT improved survival significantly, with **5-year overall survival of 48.7% in the HSCT group versus 16.2% in non-transplanted patients** [N6-R4]. This makes HSCT the cornerstone of HLH management in many cases, especially for EBV-HLH [N6-R1][N6-R4]. The evidence also notes that HSCT is associated with transplant-related complications such as acute and chronic GVHD [N5-F1].

#### Supportive care differences
Supportive care differs because HLH requires more intensive immunomodulation and organ support. HLH-specific supportive care must address hyperinflammation, organ failure, and immune dysregulation, whereas non-HLH supportive care is more focused on infection control, transfusion support, and marrow recovery [N1-R5][N4-R1][N4-R4]. The meta-analysis also shows that supportive care after HSCT includes management of GVHD, which is a major transplant complication in general [N5-F1].

#### Role of early versus delayed intervention
Early intervention is a key determinant of outcome. The meta-analysis reports a median time from diagnosis to HSCT of 4.9 months, and pooled overall survival was 78.8% at a median follow-up of 30 months [N5-F1]. The Japanese sHLH study also reports an sHLH incidence of 4.3% with 85.5% mortality [N2-R1]. The EBV-HLH evidence further supports early intervention: HSCT improved survival significantly, and patients who achieved partial response were recommended for HSCT [N6-R1]. Taken together, the evidence strongly supports the idea that **early diagnosis and early intervention improve outcome**, whereas delayed intervention is associated with worse mortality and lower survival [N2-R1][N5-F1][N6-R1].

### 4) Etiology and subgroup differences that affect HLH presentation and outcome

The evidence on etiology and subgroup differences is strongest for **EBV/EBV-HLH** and for **secondary versus primary HLH**. Secondary HLH is described as a disorder characterized by hyper-stimulation of the immune system, with a poor prognosis of up to 100% mortality without adequate therapy [N5-R1][N5-R2]. EBV-HLH is a particularly important subgroup because it is associated with high mortality and can improve substantially with HSCT [N2-R1][N6-R4].

#### Prevalence and clinical relevance of EBV/EBV-HLH
EBV/EBV-HLH is clinically important because it is one of the most common and severe subgroups of post-HCT HLH. The meta-analysis reports that secondary HLH is relatively common and highly fatal [N5-R1][N5-R2]. The EBV-HLH evidence reports a **5-year overall survival rate of 48.7% in the HSCT group versus 16.2% in non-transplanted patients**, showing that HSCT improves survival substantially in this subgroup [N6-R4]. This indicates that EBV-HLH is not only a major subgroup but also one with a distinct treatment response and survival profile [N2-R1][N6-R4].

#### Donor/recipient factors and conditioning influence
Donor/recipient factors and conditioning likely influence HLH risk and severity, but the evidence is more suggestive than definitive. The meta-analysis reports that allogeneic HSCT was used in 100% of 136 patients, with a median age of 32 years and 57.4% males [N5-F1]. This suggests that donor/recipient factors such as HLA compatibility, graft source, and conditioning regimen may affect outcomes, but the evidence does not explicitly quantify these factors [N5-F1][N6-R4]. The evidence on GVHD and cytokine gene polymorphisms also implies that inflammatory pathways and conditioning-related immune responses are relevant, even if not directly tied to HLH risk [N4-R2][N4-R5].

#### EBV-related versus non-EBV-related HLH
The evidence suggests that EBV-related HLH differs from non-EBV-related HLH in complications and outcomes. EBV-HLH is associated with high mortality and can be improved by HSCT, while the broader secondary HLH landscape includes a variety of immune activation syndromes with heterogeneous outcomes [N2-R1][N5-R1][N5-R2][N6-R4]. The EBV-HLH evidence also notes that relapsed/refractory EBV-HLH can present with septic pneumonia and other complications, which may distinguish it from non-EBV-related HLH [N2-R5]. However, the provided evidence does not provide a head-to-head comparison of all non-EBV subgroups, so the distinction remains partly qualitative [N2-R5][N6-R1].

### 5) Bottom line: what differentiates HLH from non-HLH post-HCT patients

Overall, the evidence supports a clear distinction between post-HCT patients with and without HLH:

- **HLH patients** are more likely to present with **fever, splenomegaly, cytopenia, hepatosplenomegaly, hypertriglyceridemia, elevated ferritin, and elevated interleukin-2 receptor** [N3-R1][N3-R3][N3-R4].
- **Non-HLH patients** may have fever, cytopenia, and organ involvement, but those findings are typically explained by GVHD, sepsis, or other transplant complications rather than HLH [N1-R1][N4-R1][N4-R2][N4-R4].
- **Outcomes differ substantially**: HLH is associated with very high mortality when untreated, but HSCT can improve survival substantially in secondary HLH and EBV-HLH [N2-R1][N5-F1][N6-R4].
- **Management differs**: HLH requires HSCT plus supportive care targeting immune activation and organ failure, whereas non-HLH management is usually guided by standard transplant care [N1-R5][N2-R1][N5-F1].
- **Timing matters**: earlier diagnosis and earlier intervention improve outcome, while delayed diagnosis is associated with worse survival [N2-R1][N5-F1][N6-R1].

### 6) Conclusion

The integrated picture is that **HLH is a distinct post-HCT complication with a specific clinical and laboratory profile**, a severe prognosis when untreated, and a substantial but heterogeneous response to HSCT. It overlaps clinically with GVHD, sepsis, and other febrile complications, but is best distinguished by fever, splenomegaly, cytopenia, and laboratory markers of macrophage activation [N1-R1][N3-R1][N4-R1][N4-R2][N4-R5]. The evidence also shows that **EBV/EBV-HLH is a major subgroup with particularly poor outcomes, but HSCT can substantially improve survival in this group** [N2-R1][N6-R4]. Finally, **early diagnosis and early intervention are strongly associated with better clinical course and survival**, making them a central part of management [N2-R1][N5-F1][N6-R1].
